passage:
Coach's note, college pool. Devika Nair, 3 October
Wasim trained with the 6 am group every weekday until his exams in August. Since then he hasn't been back. His locker still has his goggles and towel in it; I checked because the cleaners asked.
Today I passed him near the canteen. He saw me, went red and suddenly became very interested in his phone. When I said hello, he said, "Sorry, ma'am, I've been meaning to come. Next week, pakka." He said the same thing two weeks ago.
His friend Aman tells me Wasim changes the subject whenever swimming comes up and has stopped sitting at the café near the pool.
I don't think he's lazy. He looks embarrassed, as if coming back means facing how much ground he's lost.
What I did next: I sent him a short message. "No catching up needed. Just come on Friday and float for fifteen minutes. Your goggles are waiting."

qa.q: What is still in Wasim's locker?
Why might Wasim go red and look at his phone when he sees the coach?
qa.a: He seems ashamed of not coming back, and seeing the coach reminds him of a goal he feels he has failed.

qa.q: Why does Devika's message fit this stage?
qa.a: It removes the pressure to catch up and asks only for fifteen minutes of floating, so restarting doesn't feel like facing a failure.

qa.q: What might Aman notice about Wasim?
qa.a: Aman sees Wasim dodge any talk of swimming and avoid the café near the pool, and may be puzzled or worried by the change.

grounding: Shows a young adult avoiding a lapsed swimming routine and the coach, with shame making the return feel like confronting failure.

passage:
Sunday
The Spanish notebook is still on my desk under a pile of laundry, which is exactly where I put it so I wouldn't have to see it.
Twenty-three days since my last lesson. The app sent a reminder this morning and I swiped it away so fast.
At lunch Zubin asked, "How's the Spanish going? Say something!" I laughed, said "Hola", and asked about his internship before he could ask anything else. My face was burning.
I told everyone in July I'd be conversational by Diwali. Now opening that notebook feels like opening a report card I already know is bad. Every day I don't start, it gets heavier.
Maybe tomorrow. I wrote that yesterday too.
Ritu

qa.a: On the desk under a pile of laundry.

qa.q: Why did Ritu's face burn when Zubin asked about the Spanish?
qa.a: Ritu felt ashamed of having stopped after telling everyone about being conversational by Diwali, so the question felt like being found out.

qa.q: What small step could break the avoidance?
qa.a: Ritu could uncover the notebook and do one short lesson without trying to catch up, or tell Zubin honestly about the break and ask for company.

qa.q: What might Zubin have noticed at lunch?
qa.a: Zubin was probably just curious and friendly, and may have noticed the quick 'Hola' and change of subject without knowing the shame behind it.

grounding: Illustrates a neglected learning habit, a hidden notebook and dodged questions, where shame makes restarting feel like facing a bad report card.
